title: Organise and monitor the feeding and watering of Equines

lessons.title: Allocating feeding instructions to the team
lessons.html:
Why clear instructions matter

In a busy yard several people feed the horses: early shift, afternoon shift, weekend staff. If instructions are unclear, one horse may be fed twice and another missed, or a horse on a special diet may get the wrong feed. As the person organising feeding, you make sure every team member knows exactly what to do.

The feed chart

The feed chart is the main tool. It should be on the feed room wall and, for each horse, on the stable door.

HorseStableMorningMiddayEveningHayNotes
Duke31.5 kg cubes-1.5 kg cubes + supplement8 kgSoak hay
Bella41 kg cubes + 1 kg lucerne chaff1 kg chaff1 kg cubes10 kgOld mare, soak cubes

Feeds should be written by weight, not only scoops. Mark each scoop with the weight it holds of each feed.

Allocating tasks

  1. Know who is on duty for each shift.
  2. Give each person a clear job: who makes up feeds, who feeds which block, who fills hay nets, who checks water.
  3. Explain any changes face to face and write them on the chart, with the date and your initials.
  4. Ask the team member to repeat back important changes.
  5. Make sure new or relief staff are shown the feed room, chart and scoops before they feed.

Making up feeds

  • Use clean buckets or bowls labelled with each horse's name.
  • Make up feeds in the feed room from the chart, one horse at a time.
  • Check supplements and medication are added only where the chart says.
  • Feed horses in the same order each time, quietly, to keep them calm.

Hygiene and storage

Keep the feed room clean, dry and locked. Store feed in closed bins to keep out rats and moisture. Use older stock first. Check for mould, damp or a strange smell and never feed spoiled feed. Wash feed bowls daily.

lessons.title: Monitoring the feeding and watering plan
lessons.html:
Monitoring means checking

A good plan only works if you check that it is followed and that the horses are doing well on it.

Daily checks

  • Has every horse eaten its feed? Check bowls and mangers before the next meal. Record any feed left over.
  • Has every horse eaten its hay? A full hay net in the morning can be an early sign of illness or tooth problems.
  • Is water clean and full? Check buckets, troughs and automatic drinkers at every feed.
  • Are droppings normal in amount and consistency?
  • Are scoops being used correctly? Check one or two feeds by weighing them now and then.

Water

Water is the most important nutrient. Horses drink much more in hot weather, after work, and when lactating. Signs that a horse is not drinking enough include dry, hard droppings, dull eyes and reduced eating. A quick skin pinch test on the neck, where the skin is slow to flatten, may indicate dehydration; report it. In winter check for frozen troughs. On the veld, check that camp troughs, ball valves and windmills or pumps are working.

Records

Keep a simple daily feeding record: horse, feed eaten (all/part/none), water, and comments, signed by the groom. Review it each day. Keep stock records of feed in and used so you can order before running out.

Controlling problems

ProblemAction
Horse leaves feedCheck for illness, teeth, bad feed; report to the manager or vet
Wrong feed givenReport at once; watch the horse; correct the chart or training
Feed running lowOrder early; do not change feeds suddenly
Water not workingProvide buckets immediately and report the fault
Horse gets into the feed roomEmergency: call the vet even if the horse looks fine

lessons.title: Recognising malnutrition and overfeeding
lessons.html:
Body condition

Body condition is how much fat and muscle a horse carries. Look at and feel the neck, withers, ribs, back, and the tail head.

ConditionSigns
Too thinRibs, spine, hip bones and tail head stand out; hollow neck; dull coat
IdealRibs can be felt but not easily seen; smooth outline; shiny coat
Too fatRibs hard to feel; fat crest on the neck; fat pads around the tail head and behind the shoulder; gutter along the back

Check condition every two weeks and use a weight tape. Record the results so you can see changes over time.

Malnutrition (underfeeding)

Causes: too little feed or poor hay; bad teeth; worms; illness; bullying by other horses in a camp; hard work without enough energy.

Signs: weight loss, low energy, dull or staring coat, poor hooves, slow healing, in young horses poor growth.

Action: report to the manager; arrange a vet and dental check and deworming; increase forage first; increase concentrate gradually; feed horses that get bullied separately.

Overfeeding

Causes: too much concentrate for the work done, lush grazing, a horse that is resting but still on a full working ration.

Risks: obesity, laminitis (painful inflammation in the feet), colic, and in young horses joint and bone problems. Too much concentrate can also make a horse over-excited and difficult to handle.

Signs of laminitis: reluctance to walk, rocking back onto the heels, hot feet, a strong pulse at the back of the fetlock. This is an emergency; call the vet.

Action: report; reduce concentrate gradually; match feed to work; limit grazing time where advised; increase exercise if the horse is sound.

When work changes

If a horse is rested because of injury, the concentrate must be cut down the same day, as the manager or vet instructs, but forage continues. When work increases, increase feed gradually.

Key points

  • Allocate clear feeding jobs and keep the feed chart up to date by weight.
  • Check feed eaten, hay eaten, water and droppings every day and record them.
  • A horse in the feed room is an emergency.
  • Thin horses: check teeth, worms and illness; increase feed gradually.
  • Overfeeding causes obesity and laminitis; match feed to the work.
